content: The United Nations Secretary-General has emphasized the critical importance of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in healthcare facilities, elevating the issue to the highest levels of global attention. This call to action has been supported by the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF, which convened a global strategic meeting in May 2018 with key stakeholders to define a comprehensive response. This response includes a clear vision, measurable targets, and metrics to monitor progress. Recognizing the challenges in achieving basic WASH services in many healthcare facilities, WHO and UNICEF advocate for an incremental improvement approach. This strategy values all progressive steps toward the goal, even if initial services do not meet the basic requirements. The first objective is to provide at least some WASH services where none exist, followed by the establishment and maintenance of basic WASH services throughout the facility. These services, aligned with global standards and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), must be inclusive and equitably distributed. In facilities where basic WASH services are already in place, efforts should focus on achieving higher service levels. This includes ensuring access to safe, continuous, piped drinking water (and medical-grade water where necessary) to prevent waterborne outbreaks such as Legionella. Additionally, proper management of fecal waste is essential to mitigate risks associated with highly contagious pathogens and antimicrobial-resistant bacteria. At all service levels, environmentally sustainable solutions should be prioritized, such as reducing water wastage, installing energy-efficient water systems, and minimizing harmful emissions from healthcare waste treatment. WHO and UNICEF have also established a global network to provide technical support to countries and regions. This network is guided by an advisory group of international experts, including implementing partners, donors, policy think tanks, and academic organizations. Advocacy for WASH in healthcare facilities is integrated into existing health and WASH campaigns, as well as global observance days like World Health Day, World Water Day, and Hand Hygiene Day. The WASH in healthcare facilities knowledge portal has been revamped to focus on commitments, knowledge management, and exchange. This platform facilitates the sharing of the latest standards, tools, and approaches for improving and sustaining WASH services with national and sub-national governments and partners. Global public health security, which involves minimizing the impact of acute events that threaten population health, is increasingly critical. Recent outbreaks, such as the 2015 West Africa and 2018-2019 Democratic Republic of Congo Ebola epidemics, as well as ongoing cholera transmission in nearly 50 countries, highlight the urgent need for improved outbreak prevention and control. Factors like climate change, migration, conflict, and urbanization further complicate efforts to enhance health security. Water, sanitation, and hygiene services in healthcare facilities are fundamental to infection prevention and control, as well as the delivery of quality care. They are essential for respecting the dignity and human rights of patients and healthcare workers. Every patient and healthcare worker deserves a clean and safe environment, and no mother or child should face illness or death due to inadequate WASH services. The systems, technologies, and expertise required to provide, monitor, and sustain safe and sustainable WASH services already exist. Numerous countries are taking action on the eight practical steps outlined in this document, with thousands of communities and millions of healthcare workers globally working to improve WASH services and practices. These efforts utilize practical tools and climate-friendly approaches to enhance the quality of care. Greater collaboration, multi-sectoral planning, and implementation are needed, along with commitment, humility, and courage. At the heart of these efforts is the prevention of millions of deaths, the celebration of millions of first birthdays, increased trust and respect for healthcare workers, and healthier, stronger communities. The Global Call to Action, renewed focus on quality and primary healthcare, and the growing importance of addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) provide new momentum to tackle this solvable problem. The path forward is clear, and it is now up to us to act.
